title: Chapter 69: Peony for the Soon Departed 1
content:
Chapter 69

Peony for the Soon Departed 1

Autumn, at the Phoenix Mountain hunting grounds.

Hundreds upon hundreds of cultivators gathered in an area notoriously infested with dark spirits and foul beasts, competing within a set time limit to see who could bag the best prey. This was the grand hunt. Sprawling across several miles with undulating peaks and abundant quarry, Phoenix Mountain was celebrated as one of the three premier hunting grounds in the realm, having hosted countless legendary events. A gathering of this scale wasn't merely a stage for major and minor clans to flex their martial strength and scout fresh talent; it was an open arena for wandering rogues and ambitious newcomers to make a name for themselves overnight.

In front of the mountain stretched a vast, stone-paved plaza ringed by dozens of towering observation pavilions. The stands buzzed with an ocean of jostling spectators, electric whispers humming through the air. Naturally, the quietest tier belonged to the highest, most opulent pavilion. Seated there were esteemed elders, sect leaders, and their noble retinues. Maidens in the back held aloft embroidered canopies and feather fans, while the ladies in the front row masked their faces with painted folding fans, looking down upon the field with immaculate aristocratic poise.

However, the moment the mounted contingent of the Gusu Lan Sect trotted onto the field, all pretense of poise was thrown to the wind.

When actually hunting down prey during a night-hunt, nobody truly relied on horses. Yet horsemanship remained a mandatory pursuit for highborn disciples, serving on ceremonial occasions not only as an expression of formal etiquette, but as a surefire way to project a dazzling, coordinated spectacle. Simply put, it was all about looking proper and looking damn good. Lan Xichen and Lan Wangji rode abreast on a pair of snow-white stallions, leading the Gusu Lan formation at an unhurried, measured pace. Both carried their spiritual swords at their hips and longbows across their backs, pristine white robes and forehead ribbons fluttering in the wind like celestial immortals descended from the clouds. Their tall white riding boots were so spotlessly clean they put the clothes of the surrounding onlookers to shame. The Twin Jades of Lan truly lived up to their name—twin carvings of unblemished mutton-fat jade, chiseled from pure ice and snow. The second they crossed the threshold, the very autumn air seemed to turn crisp and sweet. The female cultivators in the stands swooned instantly. The more reserved merely lowered their fans, their eager stares growing noticeably undisguised; the bolder ones had already rushed to the railings, raining down showers of fresh blossoms they had prepared in advance. Tossing flowers to express romantic admiration toward exceptionally handsome men and women was an age-old tradition; blessed with peerless talent and striking looks, the disciples of the Gusu Lan Sect had grown desensitized to this treatment long ago. Lan Xichen and Lan Wangji in particular had been dodging flying petals since they were thirteen. Perfectly unfazed, the two offered a modest nod toward the viewing stands and continued down the path without breaking stride.

Suddenly, Lan Wangji’s hand whipped up, snatching a solitary blossom that had sailed in from behind.

Turning in his saddle, he looked toward the mounted ranks of the Yunmeng Jiang Sect waiting their turn to deploy. At the head of the formation, Jiang Cheng gave an irritated click of his tongue. Beside him, draped carelessly over the neck of a lustrous black steed, was a figure leaning on his elbows, chatting up a storm with two lithe female cultivators as if nothing had happened.

Noticing Lan Wangji had pulled on the reins, Lan Xichen asked, "Wangji, what is it?"

Lan Wangji called out flatly, "Wei Ying."

Only then did Wei Wuxian casually turn his head, feigning sheer innocence. "What's that? Hanguang-jun, were you calling me? Something the matter?"

Lan Wangji held up the flower, his face and tone coated in familiar winter frost. "Was it you?"

Wei Wuxian denied it on the spot. "Not me."

The two young women beside him ratted him out instantly. "Don't buy it, it was totally him!"

Wei Wuxian clutched his chest in mock offense. "How can you frame an upright man like this? You’re breaking my heart!"

Giggling uncontrollably, the maidens tugged their reins and wheeled their mounts back into their own formation. Lan Wangji let his hand drop, blossom in grip, and offered a resigned shake of his head. Jiang Cheng called out, "Ze-wu-jun, Hanguang-jun, pay him no mind. My apologies."

Lan Xichen chuckled. "Think nothing of it. I shall accept Young Master Wei's floral tribute on Wangji's behalf."

As the Lan contingent drifted out of earshot amidst a trailing cloud of perfumed blossoms, Jiang Cheng cast an eye at the fluttering sea of pastel silk handkerchiefs waving from the stands. He shot Wei Wuxian a dark look. "They're tossing flowers, why the hell are you joining in?"

Wei Wuxian shrugged. "Saw a pretty face and threw a couple of petals. What, is that illegal?"

Jiang Cheng sneered, "How old are you supposed to be? A man of your standing playing games like a lovesick schoolgirl."

Wei Wuxian gave him an appraising glance. "What, jealous? There are plenty on the ground. Want me to scrape a few up for you?" He leaned down in the saddle as if to grab some, and Jiang Cheng snapped, "Piss off!"

Right then, Jin Guangyao’s crisp voice echoed across the open plaza: "Announcing the mounted column of the Qinghe Nie Sect!"

Nie Mingjue was a giant of a man, imposing enough on his own two feet; mounted atop an armored warhorse, his razor-sharp aura practically suffocated the courtyard, and the chatter from the stands died down instantly. It was an unspoken rule that whenever the young masters ranked on the official bachelor charts made their entrance, they were pelted with a torrential downpour of blossoms. Seventh-ranked Nie Mingjue was the sole exception. If Lan Wangji was a sculpture of frost and snow, Nie Mingjue was ice wrapped around a raging furnace—looking as though a tidal wave of volcanic wrath could erupt from him at any second. Nobody had the suicidal urge to push his buttons. Even if the smitten maidens in the stands had hearts pounding against their ribs, their trembling fingers clutched their damp bouquets in white-knuckled terror, petrified that annoying him would result in a single saber slash bringing the entire wooden pavilion crashing down upon their heads. The male cultivators who worshiped Chifeng-zun, however, made up for the silence, bellowing cheers so loud they rattled the rafters. Riding beside him was Nie Huaisang, impeccably dressed to the nines as usual, his waist hung with jade rings, a decorative saber, and a paper folding fan lazily fluttering in his hand. At a glance, he was the spitting image of an idle, aristocratic dandy. Yet everyone knew that ornamental saber was never going to clear its scabbard today; within the hour, he'd be taking a leisurely stroll through the scenic valleys, picking wildflowers and admiring the foliage.

Following the Qinghe Nie Sect came the banner of Yunmeng Jiang.

The moment Wei Wuxian and Jiang Cheng spurred their horses forward, another relentless barrage of petals showered down upon them. It made Jiang Cheng’s face cloud over with pure aggravation, but Wei Wuxian basked in the rain of flowers with lazy delight, casually waving toward the highest observation tier. Occupying the prime seats at the summit was Madame Jin of the Lanling Jin Sect, with Jiang Yanli seated right beside her. Throughout the procession, Madame Jin had been holding her hand with doting warmth, speaking to her with deep affection. Jiang Yanli had always been an unassuming, plain-faced maiden who kept her eyes lowered with demure restraint, but seeing her two younger brothers wave from the field brought a brilliant, radiant smile across her features. Setting her painted fan aside, she murmured a few shy words to Madame Jin, walked over to the wooden balustrade, and tossed two delicate blossoms their way.

She put every ounce of her fragile strength into the throw. For a second, Wei Wuxian and Jiang Cheng held their breath, terrified she was going to tip over the rail, relaxing only when she caught her footing. Both reached out, snatching the pale violet blooms mid-air with easy smiles, pinning the petals over their hearts before continuing down the track. Countless young maidens in the stands threw burning, envious glances at Jiang Yanli as she ducked her head and slipped back to Madame Jin’s side. Just as they cleared the stands, a disciplined formation of cultivators clad in snow-white robes embroidered with gilded motifs burst onto the field, their light breastplates gleaming atop magnificent stallions. Leading the charge at the very front was none other than the sect leader himself, Jin Guangshan.

Madame Jin immediately patted Jiang Yanli’s shoulder, pulling her back to the rail to point toward the approaching golden ranks.

Amidst a flurry of proud whinnies, a lone rider broke formation, galloping in a triumphant lap around the stone plaza before sharply reining in his mount. The youth sat tall and elegant in the saddle, his white robes spotless as fresh snow. The vermilion mark centered on his brow was entirely outshined by his dazzling, striking features. Drawing his golden bow with effortless martial poise, he sent the observation stands into a deafening frenzy. His gaze drifted casually across the stands, and though he fought to maintain an unbothered, stoic face, the smug pride oozing from the corner of his lips was impossible to conceal.

Wei Wuxian snorted, nearly laughing himself out of the saddle. "I have to hand it to the guy. Look at him, strutting around like a puffed-up peacock."

Jiang Cheng muttered, "Keep it in check. A-Jie is watching from the pavilion."

Wei Wuxian waved him off. "Relax. So long as he doesn't bring her to tears again, I couldn't care less about him. You shouldn't have brought her here in the first place."

Jiang Cheng frowned. "The Lanling Jin Sect sent a formal, insistent invitation. We couldn't afford the loss of face."

Wei Wuxian scoffed, "You mean Madame Jin insisted. Mark my words, she’s going to spend the whole afternoon scheming ways to shove our shijie into a corner with that spoiled prince."

While they bickered, Jin Zixuan had already trotted up to the archery barrier. This row of targets stood as the formal gatekeeper to the mountains; every participant had to pierce a target from a designated distance before being granted entry to the hunt. Seven concentric rings marked each target, corresponding to seven different mountain trails. The closer an arrow landed to the bullseye, the more advantageous the allocated trail. Without slowing his steed an inch, Jin Zixuan smoothly drew a fletched shaft from his quiver, drew the bowstring taut, and loosed. The arrow slammed dead-center into the crimson mark. Cheers erupted across the stands.

Watching him soak in the limelight, neither Wei Wuxian nor Jiang Cheng batted an eye. Suddenly, a loud, deliberate snort broke out nearby, followed by an arrogant bark: "If anyone on this field thinks they're hot shit, step right up and try beating Zixuan's shot!"

The speaker was tall, broad-shouldered, and swarthy, his booming voice carrying across the ranks. It was Jin Zixun, Jin Guangshan’s nephew and Jin Zixuan’s cousin. Ever since Wei Wuxian’s heated clash with Jin Zixuan during the flower banquet at Koi Tower, Jin Zixun had been nursing a petty grudge, and now he was fishing for a fight. Wei Wuxian merely offered an amused smirk. Seeing no rebuttal, Jin Zixun’s face filled with greasy satisfaction. When the Yunmeng Jiang contingent finally rolled up before the targets, Wei Wuxian glanced sideways at the Twin Jades of Lan, who were currently checking their strings. "Lan Zhan, do me a favor?"

Lan Wangji’s pale gaze flicked over, silent as stone. Jiang Cheng snapped, "What are you pulling now?"

Lan Wangji asked, "What is it?"

Wei Wuxian grinned. "Lend me your forehead ribbon?"

The second the words cleared his mouth, Lan Wangji snapped his gaze forward, refusing to spare him another glance. Lan Xichen chuckled, offering, "Young Master Wei, you may not be aware..."

Lan Wangji cut him off cleanly: "Brother, leave it."

Lan Xichen relented. "Very well."

Jiang Cheng was on the verge of smacking Wei Wuxian right off his horse. The bastard knew damn well that Lan Wangji would never hand over his ribbon, yet he insisted on poking the bear purely to cause chaos. If hundreds of people weren't watching, Jiang Cheng swore he’d have throttled him on the spot. "What the hell do you need a ribbon for? Planning to hang yourself? I can lend you a sash, no charge."

Wei Wuxian began unwrapping the black bracer ties from his wrist, tossing back, "Keep your sash. If I can't have his ribbon, I certainly don't want your rags."

Jiang Cheng bristled. "You—!"

Before the insult landed, Wei Wuxian snapped the black ribbon tight around his eyes, blindfolding himself in one fluid motion. Nock, draw, release—thump!

Bullseye!

The entire sequence unfolded with the seamless, blinding speed of a crack of lightning. The crowd hadn't even processed what he was doing before the red center of the distant target had a shaft punched clean through its core. A beat of stunned, dead silence hung over the field, shattered an instant later by an earth-shattering wave of roaring cheers—far louder and wildly more fervent than the applause Jin Zixuan had received moments before.

A roguish smirk curled Wei Wuxian’s lips. He spun the bow lightly across his knuckles and tossed it behind him. Seeing his cousin outshined so thoroughly, Jin Zixun’s face turned an ugly, sour shade of green. He spat, "Just a flashy opening shot! Anyone can pull off empty tricks. If you're so damn confident, why don't you keep that blindfold on for the entire hunt? Let's see you put your money where your mouth is on Phoenix Mountain!"

Wei Wuxian chuckled. "Deal."

Jin Zixun barked a sharp command, waving his hand: "Move out!"

His retinue spurred their mounts forward in a mad dash, desperate to breach the perimeter first and sweep up the highest-tier game before anyone else had a chance. Seeing his clan's cavalry charge out with disciplined precision, Jin Guangshan smiled smugly. Catching sight of Wei Wuxian and Jiang Cheng still idling in their saddles, he called out with oily warmth, "Sect Leader Jiang, Young Master Wei, not joining the fray? Careful now, or Zixun might just bag all the prize beasts before you get through the gate."

Wei Wuxian replied breezily, "No rush. He won't be taking them."

The onlookers blinked in confusion. While Jin Guangshan was still turning over what on earth "won't be taking them" was supposed to mean, Wei Wuxian rolled out of the saddle, turning to Jiang Cheng. "Go ahead without me."

Jiang Cheng muttered, "Keep it reasonable. Don't go too far."

Wei Wuxian flicked a casual wrist in goodbye. Jiang Cheng cracked his reins, leading the Yunmeng Jiang contingent galloping into the brush.

Left behind, Wei Wuxian kept his eyes bound in black, resting his hands behind his back as he took a lazy, unhurried stroll down the mountain trail. He looked less like a competitor joining a dangerous monster hunt and more like an idle lord taking a scenic walk through his private gardens.

The crowd exchanged baffled looks. Is he seriously keeping that blindfold on for the entire hunt? How the hell is he supposed to track anything like that?

Shrugging it off as none of their business, the remaining cultivators scattered into the wilderness to hunt down their own glory.

After ambling solo for a good long while, Wei Wuxian finally stumbled upon the ideal spot to catch a nap deep within the remote ridges of Phoenix Mountain.

A massive branch branched out horizontally from an ancient, gnarled trunk, blocking his path. Patting the weathered bark and finding it completely sturdy, he hopped up with feline grace, settling against the boughs.

The deafening roar of the spectator pavilions had long been swallowed by the dense sea of pines. Leaning back against the timber, Wei Wuxian closed his eyes behind the dark cloth, feeling the dappled autumn sunlight filtering through the canopy to warm his cheeks.

He retrieved Chenqing from his lapel, brought the dark bamboo to his lips, and let his breath flow. A bright, haunting melody soared into the sky like a startling bird, rippling through the valleys and riding the wind into the deep woods.

Dangling one leg off the bough, he gently swung his boot to the rhythm. The leather toe brushed through the dewy fern fronds below, completely unbothered as the morning moisture soaked into the fabric.

As the final note faded, he crossed his arms, shifting into an even lazier slouch against the bark. The flute was tucked safely into his robes, while the pale violet blossom from Jiang Yanli remained pinned over his heart, exhaling a faint, clean fragrance.

He lounged there for who knows how long, drifting right on the edge of sleep, when a sudden prickle of awareness snapped him wide awake.

Footsteps. Someone was approaching.

Sensing zero killing intent from the visitor, he couldn't be bothered to sit up, let alone peel off the blindfold. He merely tilted his head toward the rustling leaves.

A long silence stretched between them, neither offering a word. Wei Wuxian broke the quiet with an amused drawl: "Here for the hunt?"

No answer.

"Hate to break it to you," Wei Wuxian continued, "but you won't find a scrap of game anywhere near me."

Still, the stranger offered not a single syllable, though the soft crunch of dry twigs signaled a few steps forward.

Now Wei Wuxian was genuinely intrigued. Most cultivators gave him a wide berth out of sheer dread; people rarely dared step into his shadow in broad daylight, let alone corner him alone in a desolate wood. If not for the complete lack of bloodlust, he’d have suspected an ambush. He straightened his spine a fraction, turning his covered face toward the footsteps. Smirking, he was just opening his mouth to toss out another tease when an unexpected, violent shove caught him squarely in the chest.

Thud!

His back slammed hard against the tree trunk. His right hand whipped up to tear the blindfold off, but the stranger's grip clamped around his wrist like an iron vise—pinning it down with monstrous strength that he couldn't shake off. Yet even now, the intruder radiated zero malice. Wei Wuxian’s left sleeve twitched, flicking a spiritual talisman into his palm, but the stranger saw right through him, seizing that wrist as well and pinning both of his arms flat against the bark with bruising, unyielding force. Wei Wuxian coiled his leg, preparing to plant a vicious kick into their ribs, when a sudden, soft warmth pressed against his lips.

He froze.

The sensation was unfamiliar, jarring, and searingly hot. His mind blanked out completely; for several dizzying seconds, his brain couldn't process what was happening.

Someone had him pinned against a tree by his wrists, and was kissing him.

A jolt of adrenaline kicked in; he thrashed wildly to yank his arms free and rip the blindfold away, but the iron grip refused to budge. He braced to summon his demonic energy, then caught himself dead in his tracks.

The person kissing him... was trembling.

A fragile, quiet shudder ran through the body pressing against his.

And just like that, all the fight melted out of Wei Wuxian’s limbs.

Man, he thought, bewildered, this girl’s got a grip like a bear trap, but she’s scared out of her mind. Shaking like a leaf. Why else would she ambush him like this? She must have mustered every scrap of courage she had just to sneak this moment. Judging by that inhuman spiritual strength, she clearly possessed formidable cultivation, which meant her pride had to be astronomical. If he tore the blindfold off right now and stared her in the face, how mortified would she be?

Two sets of lips brushed and shifted, delicate and agonizingly hesitant, tangled in a messy, breathless hesitation. Before Wei Wuxian could figure out whether to play along or pull back, the tender kiss turned predatory.

His guard dropped; the stranger parted his lips, forcing their way past his teeth with sudden, overwhelming fervor. Wei Wuxian was left completely defenseless. His lungs screamed for air, and he tried to turn his face aside, only for a firm hand to cup his jaw, forcefully dragging his mouth back to meet the onslaught. His senses spun out of control as their tongues tangled, a dizzying heat rushing straight to his head.

A sharp nip caught his lower lip, followed by a lingering, desperate nuzzle, before the stranger finally, reluctantly pulled away.

Wei Wuxian slumped limply against the tree, his knees completely shot through. It took several long seconds before the strength trickled back into his arms.

His hand flew up, ripping the black ribbon away. The blinding autumn sun seared his pupils, forcing him to squint against the sting. When his vision finally cleared, the clearing was dead empty. Tangled brush, ancient pines, wild weeds, withered vines.

Not a single soul in sight.

Still half-dazed, Wei Wuxian lingered on the branch for a moment before dropping to the ground. The second his boots hit the dirt, his knees buckled, an embarrassing wave of dizziness washing over him.

He hastily leaned against the trunk to steady himself, mentally cursing his own pathetic lack of stamina—getting kissed until he couldn't even stand on his own two feet! Scanning the timber, there wasn't a single snapped twig or fresh footprint to trace. The whole ordeal felt like a bizarre, intoxicating daydream, the kind of wanton illusion born of woodland spirits and mischievous forest sprites from local folklore.

Yet he knew with absolute certainty that this was no woodland demon. It was a living, breathing human being.

Recalling the heat of those lips, a strange, phantom flutter brushed against his ribs. Reaching up to touch his chest, his fingers met bare fabric.

The pale violet flower was gone.

He swept the grass beneath the tree, but turned up nothing. It hadn't fallen—it had been taken.

Wei Wuxian stood there in stunned silence, his fingers drifting up to graze his swollen lips. After an eternity, he choked out a single, exasperated breath:

"Unbelievable... That was my damn..."

After sweeping the immediate perimeter and turning up empty, Wei Wuxian didn't know whether to laugh or cry. Accepting that the mystery maiden was clearly avoiding him and wouldn't show her face again, he began wandering aimlessly through the timber. Before he'd gotten far, a thunderous crash echoed from a clearing ahead. Looking up, his eyes landed on a tall, familiar silhouette draped in pristine white robes.

Who else could it be but Lan Wangji?

Yet while the body undeniably belonged to Lan Wangji, the behavior was an absolute anomaly.

When Wei Wuxian laid eyes on him, Lan Wangji was driving a bare-knuckled fist straight into the trunk of an ancient pine—snapping the thick wood clean in two with raw, concussive force.

Wei Wuxian blinked, thoroughly baffled. "Lan Zhan! What are you doing?"

The figure whipped around. Sure enough, it was Lan Wangji. Yet faint, crimson capillaries were spider-webbing through his pale eyes, his expression borderline feral. Wei Wuxian raised an eyebrow, genuinely startled. "Whoa. Remind me never to get on your bad side."

Lan Wangji’s voice was venomously sharp: "Leave!"

Wei Wuxian protested, "I literally just walked up and you're already chasing me away? Do you really despise me that much?"

Lan Wangji ground out, "Stay away from me!"

Aside from those frantic, feverish days trapped beneath the earth with the Xuanwu of Slaughter, Wei Wuxian had never seen Lan Wangji lose his composure like this. Back then, they were battered, broken, and starving, which made the outbursts understandable; what on earth could have set him off in the middle of a peaceful hunt?

Taking a cautious step back, Wei Wuxian put his hands up, keeping his distance. "Alright, alright, I'm staying back. But seriously, Lan Zhan, what happened to you? Are you alright? If something's wrong, just spit it out."

Refusing to meet his eyes, Lan Wangji drew Bichen. A brilliant arc of icy blue sword-glare whistled through the clearing, scything through the surrounding pines; seconds later, the timber came crashing down with a deafening groan.

He stood frozen amidst the fallen trees, his white knuckles gripping the hilt so hard the bones threatened to burst through the skin. Slowly, his jagged breathing began to level out. Then, his head snapped back up, his unblinking stare boring straight into Wei Wuxian’s face.

Wei Wuxian felt deeply uneasy. Having kept his eyes bound in pitch-black silk for over an hour, the daylight was still harsh against his pupils, leaving his eyes watery and red-rimmed. Combined with his visibly swollen, bruised lips, he knew he looked like an absolute disaster right now. Shifting under the intense scrutiny, he rubbed his chin awkwardly. "...Lan Zhan?"

"..."

Lan Wangji’s voice was flat: "It is nothing."

With a crisp, metallic chime, Bichen clicked back into its scabbard. Lan Wangji spun on his heel, walking away without a backward glance. Still convinced something was dreadfully wrong, Wei Wuxian jogged to catch up, reaching out with a quick grappling flick to catch his wrist and check his meridians. Lan Wangji sidestepped the grab with practiced ease, leveling a frigid glare at him.

Wei Wuxian raised his hands defensively. "Don't look at me like I'm a criminal. I just wanted to make sure you weren't dying. You're acting bizarre today. You sure you didn't get poisoned by some foul beast or catch some nasty curse?"

Lan Wangji answered clipped, "No."

Seeing the frost smooth back over his features, it seemed the storm had truly passed. A breath of relief escaped Wei Wuxian's lungs; realizing it was poor manners to keep prying into someone's private business, he switched gears to mindless chatter. Lan Wangji ignored him at first, though he eventually relented, tossing back a few curt, monosyllabic replies.

Yet the lingering heat and dull ache throbbed relentlessly against Wei Wuxian’s lips, serving as a constant, burning reminder:

He had just surrendered the first kiss he’d guarded for twenty damn years—kissed until his head spun and his knees turned to water—and he didn't even have the faintest clue who she was or what she looked like.

It was downright infuriating.

Wei Wuxian let out a lazy, drawn-out sigh, and completely out of the blue, asked, "Hey, Lan Zhan—have you ever kissed anyone?"

If Jiang Cheng had been around to hear him blurt out something so absurd and frivolous, he would have delivered a fist straight to his jaw without a second thought.

Lan Wangji stopped dead in his tracks. His voice, when he finally spoke, was so cold it was practically brittle: "Why do you ask?"

Wei Wuxian broke into a knowing, triumphant grin.

"Never, right?" he said, squinting teasingly. "I knew it! Just asking off the cuff, no need to get so worked up."

Lan Wangji asked, "How could you know?"

"Isn't it obvious?" Wei Wuxian laughed. "With that permanent scowl of yours, who on earth would dare plant one on you? And heaven knows you’d never take the initiative yourself. Guess you're guarding that first kiss for the rest of your days! Hahah..."

He was thoroughly enjoying his own little joke, while Lan Wangji just stood there, expressionless. Yet, almost imperceptibly, the harsh tension in his face seemed to soften.

Once Wei Wuxian had laughed his fill, Lan Wangji asked quietly, "And you?"

Wei Wuxian arched a brow, smugness radiating off him in waves. "Me? Do you even need to ask? I'm a seasoned veteran, of course."

Any warmth that had just settled into Lan Wangji’s expression instantly froze over, buried beneath an arctic blizzard.

Just then, Wei Wuxian cut himself off with a sharp, "Shh!"

He perked up, intently tracking a faint disturbance in the trees, then caught Lan Wangji’s arm and yanked him down behind a dense thicket of bushes.

Lan Wangji, having no clue what this sudden panic was about, was just parting his lips to demand an explanation when he caught Wei Wuxian’s laser-focused stare. Following his line of sight, he spotted two silhouettes emerging from beneath the emerald canopy—one draped in white, the other in violet, walking one behind the other.

The young man leading the way was tall and impeccably handsome, though practically dripping with arrogant, overbearing disdain. Marked by a vermilion dot centered on his brow, his snow-white robes were trimmed in opulent gold, his countless gemstone accessories flashing brilliantly under the dappled sunlight. Head held high, he strutted forward with an insufferable swagger: Jin Zixuan. Trailing behind him was a petite, slender maiden taking quiet, tentative steps, head bowed in total silence. Standing in stark contrast to his grand display, it was none other than Jiang Yanli.

I knew it, Wei Wuxian thought, rolling his eyes. Madame Jin definitely schemed to get Shijie and that golden peacock alone together.

Beside him, Lan Wangji caught the blatant contempt twisting his features and murmured under his breath, "What grievance do you bear against Jin Zixuan?"

Wei Wuxian only scoffed.

If anyone wanted to trace the bad blood between Wei Wuxian and Jin Zixuan, they'd have to unpack an exhausting, generational grudge.

Madam Yu and Jin Zixuan’s mother, Madame Jin, had been thick as thieves since girlhood. Way back when, they’d made a pact: if they both had sons, the boys would swear brotherhood; if both had daughters, they’d become sisters; and if they had a boy and a girl, they would be husband and wife.

The matriarchs shared an ironclad bond, knew each other's families inside and out, and matched each other flawlessly in status. By every metric of high society, this arranged betrothal was a match made in heaven—everyone celebrated it as a match destined by the gods. Unfortunately, the two kids saddled with it begged to differ.

From the day he drew breath, Jin Zixuan had been pampered, adored, and placed on a silver pedestal. Fair-skinned, blessed with that signature vermilion mark, noble-blooded, and brilliant to a fault, he was universally fawned over, growing up with an unbearable streak of pure arrogance. Whenever Madame Jin brought him over to Lotus Pier for visits, neither Wei Wuxian nor Jiang Cheng could stand being in the same room with him. Only Jiang Yanli would fuss over him, patiently trying to offer him home-cooked treats—which Jin Zixuan consistently ignored with cold indifference, sending Wei Wuxian and Jiang Cheng into howling fits of childish rage.

Years later, Wei Wuxian threw down and raised hell at the Cloud Recesses, thoroughly smashing the engagement between the Jiang and Jin clans to pieces. When he returned to Lotus Pier, he had bowed his head to apologize to his Shijie, but Jiang Yanli hadn't uttered a single word of reproach, merely stroking his hair with gentle affection. Both Wei Wuxian and Jiang Cheng had genuinely assumed the storm had passed—that breaking the cursed match was a win for everyone involved. It was only much later that they realized she had likely been nursing a shattered heart the entire time.

Halfway through the Sunshot Campaign, the Yunmeng Jiang Sect marched out to reinforce the Lanling Jin forces around Langya. With manpower stretched razor-thin across the frontlines, Jiang Yanli had insisted on following them onto the battlefield.

Knowing full well her spiritual cultivation was modest, she took on whatever she could manage, sweating away in the encampment kitchens to prepare meals for the frontline cultivators. Wei Wuxian and Jiang Cheng had pushed back aggressively at first, but cooking was her passion, she got along famously with the other volunteers, and keeping her away from direct combat kept her safe and unburdened. Seeing her happy, they eventually let it be.

Field rations during the war were notoriously grim, and Jiang Yanli worried endlessly that her two picky younger brothers would starve. So, every single day, she’d slip away to brew two extra bowls of nourishing soup specifically for Wei Wuxian and Jiang Cheng. What nobody else realized, however, was that she had quietly added a third portion to her daily labor—delivering it straight to Jin Zixuan, who was stationed at Langya as well.

Even Jin Zixuan had been completely kept in the dark. He adored the soup and was deeply moved by the anonymous kindness, but Jiang Yanli never once left her name. Little did she know, her secret had caught the calculating eye of a low-ranking female cultivator. This woman, a servant of the Lanling Jin Clan whose modest spiritual aptitude had relegated her to the exact same kitchen duties, was reasonably pretty, possessed a sharp knack for sniffing out loopholes, and quickly put the pieces together after shadowing Jiang Yanli a few times. Biding her time, she engineered an opportunity: the moment Jiang Yanli dropped off the soup and slipped away, she deliberately loitered outside Jin Zixuan’s quarters, ensuring the young master caught sight of her silhouette.

Having finally caught his mystery benefactor, Jin Zixuan demanded answers. The woman played him brilliantly—never outright claiming the credit, but blushing furiously while stumbling over coy, evasive denials, leaving the heavy impression that she was the one behind it all, merely too bashful to let him see through her humble devotion. Taking the bait, Jin Zixuan stopped pressing for a confession, but his actions spoke volumes: he began favoring her with blatant consideration, watching over her until he eventually promoted her from a common servant to a respected guest disciple. Jiang Yanli remained oblivious to the deception for weeks, right up until the afternoon she dropped off the soup—only to collide head-on with Jin Zixuan, who had unexpectedly doubled back to retrieve an urgent dispatch.

Naturally, Jin Zixuan confronted her on the spot, demanding to know what business she had skulking around his private quarters. Terrified of a scene, Jiang Yanli tried to brush it off, but as his tone grew increasingly suspicious and harsh, she had no choice but to confess the truth.

Unfortunately for her, that exact script had already been claimed.

The fallout was an absolute disaster.

Jin Zixuan wasted no time "exposing" her shameless "lies." Jiang Yanli had never imagined a simple pot of soup could spawn such a monstrous misunderstanding. Quiet and unassuming by nature, she kept such a low profile that half the camp didn't even realize she was the prized daughter of the Yunmeng Jiang Clan, leaving her with zero hard evidence to clear her name. The more she scrambled to defend herself, the more his disgusted sneer chilled her to the bone. In the end, Jin Zixuan leveled a brutal, biting verdict right at her: "Do not think your noble birth grants you the right to steal and trample upon the sincere heart of another! There are those of humble origins whose moral character far eclipses your own. Have some self-respect."

Every cruel implication in that speech hit Jiang Yanli like a hammer.

From day one, Jin Zixuan had never believed a low-cultivation maiden like her could genuinely contribute anything of value to a bloody war effort. Plainly put, he assumed she had only tagged along as an excuse to throw herself at him—a useless nuisance making a mess of things.

He had never understood her, and he’d certainly never bothered trying to. So why would he ever believe her now?

Berated and publicly humiliated, Jiang Yanli stood paralyzed, finally bursting into inconsolable sobs. That was the exact sight that greeted Wei Wuxian the second he stepped into camp.

His Shijie had the patience of a saint. Aside from the day Lotus Pier was reduced to ash—when the three surviving siblings had collapsed into each other's arms, weeping until their throats were raw—she had never shed a tear in public, let alone broken down into breathless, jagged wails before a gaping crowd. Wei Wuxian went into an absolute, blind panic. He frantically pressed her for answers, but her sobs choked her words to splinters. Then his eyes drifted toward the dazed, defensive stance of Jin Zixuan standing nearby. Rage detonated in his skull: Why is it always this bastard?! Charging forward, he planted a flying kick straight into Jin Zixuan's ribs, and an earth-shattering brawl tore through the camp. The two fought so viciously that every cultivator stationed in the area rushed out to pull them apart. Amidst the chaotic shouting, the truth was finally dragged into the open. Wei Wuxian’s fury burned even hotter—vowing bloody murder on Jin Zixuan’s life while dragging the conniving maidservant out by her collar. A brutal confrontation left the scheme stripped bare, and Jin Zixuan stood frozen, stiff as a corpse. As Wei Wuxian continued tearing into him, Jin Zixuan’s face drained to an ashen green; he didn't utter a single defense, taking the hits without raising a fist. If Jiang Yanli hadn't grabbed Wei Wuxian’s trembling wrist, and if Jiang Cheng and Jin Guangshan hadn't sprinted back to pull him off, Jin Zixuan wouldn't even be breathing well enough to ride a horse at Phoenix Mountain today.

Following the fallout, Jiang Yanli remained at Langya to finish her kitchen duties, but she kept to her lane with rigid propriety—never brewing another drop of soup for Jin Zixuan, refusing to spare him so much as a passing glance. Once the crisis in Langya subsided, Wei Wuxian and Jiang Cheng whisked her straight back home to Yunmeng. Ironically, whether driven by gnawing guilt or subjected to a blistering tongue-lashing from his mother, Jin Zixuan began incessantly inquiring after Jiang Yanli the moment the Sunshot Campaign drew to a close.

Most outsiders who caught wind of the drama brushed it off as a harmless misunderstanding—now that the air was cleared, what was the big deal? But Wei Wuxian wasn't having a single word of it. He utterly despised that self-important golden peacock, that pampered little princess, that blind hypocrite who couldn't see past a pretty face. He had zero faith that an arrogant narcissist like Jin Zixuan was capable of genuine remorse; this sudden display of lingering interest was almost certainly the result of Madame Jin screaming in his ear until he reluctantly dragged his boots out to fulfill his diplomatic duty.

Still, personal hatred aside, Wei Wuxian kept his head down to save his Shijie from an awkward scene. Beside him, Lan Wangji cast an inquisitive, sideways glance, seemingly baffled by the hostility. Wei Wuxian had no time to explain, simply pressing an index finger to his lips in a sharp "shh" while keeping his eyes glued to the clearing. Lan Wangji’s pale gaze lingered for an extra second on those flushed, swollen lips before quietly looking away.

Over in the clearing, Jin Zixuan kicked back a tangle of brush, revealing the thick carcass of a serpentine monster. Leaning down to inspect it, he muttered, "Dead."

Jiang Yanli gave a quiet nod.

"A Stature Snake," he noted.

"Pardon?" she asked softly.

Jin Zixuan explained, "A beast native to the southern wilderness. When it encounters travelers, it rears straight up to measure its length against them. If it stands taller than the person, it swallows them whole. Nothing special, just ugly."

Jiang Yanli blinked, clearly bewildered as to why he was suddenly offering an impromptu ecology lecture. By societal rules, an accomplished young lady ought to chime in with a few polite platitudes—something along the lines of Young Master Jin is so widely read or Young Master Jin is so remarkably composed. But what he had just rattled off was the most laughably basic field trivia; it was painfully obvious he was desperately fishing for conversation. Dishing out that brand of transparent flattery was a parlor trick only Jin Guangyao could pull off with a straight face, so Jiang Yanli settled for another polite nod. Wei Wuxian guessed she’d probably been nodding like a porcelain doll the entire hike.

An excruciating silence settled over the trees, the secondhand awkwardness practically radiating through the foliage to slap both men hiding in the bushes. After what felt like an eternity, Jin Zixuan finally turned to lead her back down the trail, though he couldn't keep his mouth shut for three paces: "This particular Stature Snake was heavily armored with overlapping scales, and its fangs extended past its jawline. Likely a mutated variant. Ordinary hunters would have struggled against it—standard spiritual arrows wouldn't pierce that hide."

He paused, throwing on an aggressively nonchalant tone: "Still, hardly impressive. None of the prey selected for this grand hunt amounts to much. Not a single beast out here could lay a scratch on our Lanling disciples."

Hearing that familiar, puffed-up arrogance bleeding back into his voice made Wei Wuxian's teeth ache. Glancing over, he noticed Lan Wangji staring deadpan at Jin Zixuan's retreating back. Puzzled, Wei Wuxian tracked his gaze, only to find himself fighting a bark of laughter: Since when does that bastard walk with the posture of an awkward, marching wooden toy?!

Jiang Yanli murmured, "It is best that no one gets hurt during a hunt."

"What value is there in prey that poses no danger?" Jin Zixuan countered. "If you visited the private hunting grounds of the Lanling Jin Sect, you'd see rare quarry you could never find out here."

Like hell she wants to visit your damn backyard! Wei Wuxian sneered internally.

Oblivious to the disdain, Jin Zixuan made the executive decision entirely on his own: "I happen to have an opening in my schedule next month. I could take you."

Jiang Yanli’s voice remained soft and polite: "I thank Young Master Jin for his generosity. But there is no need to trouble yourself."

Jin Zixuan froze, blurting out, "Why?"

How on earth was she supposed to answer that? Looking visibly uncomfortable, Jiang Yanli dropped her gaze to the pine needles.

Jin Zixuan pressed, "Do you dislike spectating hunts?"

Jiang Yanli gave a tiny nod.

"Then why did you come today?"

If Madame Jin hadn't practically dragged her onto the carriage by her wrist, she never would have set foot near Phoenix Mountain—but how could she possibly say that to his face?

Met with her stubborn silence, Jin Zixuan’s expression cycled violently between burning scarlet and bruised pale. His pride thoroughly mangled, he choked out a rigid, defensive bite: "Do you dislike the hunt, or do you simply loathe being near me?!"

Jiang Yanli whispered, "It is not..."

Wei Wuxian knew her heart inside out: she was worried Jin Zixuan was only inviting her out of filial obligation to appease his mother, and she had no desire to force his hand. But Jin Zixuan couldn't read between the lines to save his life. All his aristocratic brain registered was that he was enduring the single greatest humiliation of his entire life—not only was this his first time getting rejected by a maiden, it was his first time getting rejected after inviting one! Humiliation flared straight into incandescent rage. After a suffocating beat, he let out a venomous, mocking laugh. "Fine."

"My apologies," Jiang Yanli murmured.

"What do you have to apologize for?!" he spat, cold and dismissive. "Think whatever you like. It's not as though I genuinely wanted to invite you anyway. If you don't want to go, forget it!"

The blood rushed straight to Wei Wuxian's skull. He nearly charged out from behind the thicket to beat the peacock black and blue on the spot, but forced himself down. Let her see him for the spoiled brat he is, he reasoned through gritted teeth. The sooner she writes him off, the sooner she can wash her hands of him.

Jiang Yanli’s lips gave a faint, fragile quiver, but she held her tongue. Offering him a modest, formal curtsy, she whispered, "Please excuse me."

She turned and began making the trek back down the trail entirely on her own. Jin Zixuan stood rooted in place, glaring off into the trees with stiff fury. After a few beats, his patience snapped: "Hold it!"

Jiang Yanli didn't stop. Furious, Jin Zixuan closed the distance in three aggressive strides, reaching out to seize her wrist—only for a dark blur to flash before his eyes. Before his mind could register the ambush, a crushing palm strike drove straight into his sternum! Drawing his sword to parry the momentum, Jin Zixuan skidded several paces back across the dirt.

Looking up, he roared, "Wei Wuxian! Why the hell is it always you?!"

Planting himself squarely in front of Jiang Yanli like an iron wall, Wei Wuxian snarled back, "I was just about to ask the same damn thing—why the hell is it always you?!"

"Attacking me out of nowhere—have you lost your mind?!"

Wei Wuxian threw another concussive strike, his voice dripping venom: "I'm hitting exactly who I intended to hit! What do you mean 'out of nowhere'?! You got your petty feelings hurt, so you decided to lay your hands on my Shijie?!"

Jin Zixuan dodged the blow, whipping his blade around to counter. "If I didn't grab her, was I supposed to let her wander through a monster-infested forest alone?!"

The whistling arc of golden sword-glare was suddenly knocked wildly off course, its lethal edge redirected harmlessly into the clouds above. Blinking through the aftershocks, Jin Zixuan gasped, "Hanguang-jun?!"

Lan Wangji slid Bichen cleanly back into its scabbard, planting himself like a silent, immovable barrier between the two camps. Wei Wuxian stepped forward to press the attack, but Jiang Yanli caught his sleeve in a frantic grip. "A-Xian!..."

Right on cue, a chaotic rush of pounding boots shattered the quiet. A massive entourage came barreling down the trail, the lead cultivator shouting, "What happened?!"

The clash of Bichen and Suihua had launched twin pillars of spiritual energy straight into the sky, alerting every hunting party in the sector. Knowing a duel had broken out, the nearby cultivators had scrambled to converge, stumbling upon the bizarre four-way standoff. As luck would have it, the loudmouth leading the pack was none other than Jin Zixun.

"Zixuan!" he barked. "Is this Wei bastard giving you grief again?!"

Jin Zixuan frowned, waving a dismissive hand. "Stay out of this, it's none of your concern!" Seeing Wei Wuxian turning to lead Jiang Yanli away, he snapped, "Stand your ground!"

Wei Wuxian threw a glare over his shoulder. "You actually want a brawl? Let's go!"

Jin Zixun stepped up, puffing out his chest. "Wei Wuxian, you’ve picked fights with Zixuan time and time again—what are you playing at?!"

Wei Wuxian cast a disinterested sweep over him. "Who are you supposed to be?"

Jin Zixun froze, then exploded into pure, red-faced fury: "You don't know who I am?!"

Wei Wuxian blinked in genuine confusion. "Why on earth should I know who you are?"

Back when the Sunshot Campaign ignited, Jin Zixun had hidden behind a minor injury to lounge safely in the rear reserves. He had never witnessed Wei Wuxian's terrifying display on the frontlines firsthand, brushing off the battlefield rumors as gross exaggerations. Worse, Wei Wuxian had just used his flute to summon the dark spirits across the mountain, hijacking a pack of fierce corpses his party had spent hours tracking, making them look like absolute fools. Now, having this rogue demand his identity to his face felt like an intolerable, public slap. Grating on his fragile ego, he opened his mouth to unleash a tirade when golden sword-glare illuminated the clearing from above.

A second party descended gracefully onto the grass, led by a striking, sharp-featured noblewoman. She carried herself with the fierce martial pride of a seasoned warrior while radiating the effortless, regal elegance of high nobility.

Jin Zixun bowed instantly. "Aunt!"

Jin Zixuan blinked in surprise. "Mother! Why are you here?" Then reality set in: the twin sword-beams had cleaved the heavens; of course his mother had spotted them from the observation deck. Eyeing the platoon of Lanling Jin enforcers trailing behind her, he muttered, "Why did you bring so many people? I don't need you meddling in my hunt."

Madame Jin spat, "Don't flatter yourself! Who said I came out here looking for you?!"

Catching sight of Jiang Yanli shrinking behind Wei Wuxian's shoulder, her frosty demeanor melted into instant warmth. Stepping forward, she gathered the girl's trembling hands into hers, coaxing gently, "A-Li, what on earth happened to you?"

Jiang Yanli bowed her head. "Thank you for your concern, Madame. I am fine."

Madame Jin was far too sharp to buy it. Her eyes narrowed. "Did that wretched boy bully you again?"

Jiang Yanli stammered, "No, he didn't."

Jin Zixuan shifted uncomfortably, parting his lips as if to defend himself, but thought better of it. Knowing her son's rotten temper like the back of her hand, Madame Jin pieced the picture together in a heartbeat. Her fury detonated: "Jin Zixuan! Are you looking for an early grave?! What did you promise me before you walked out of that pavilion?!"

Jin Zixuan’s jaw clenched. "I—!"

Wei Wuxian cut in, his voice dripping with ice: "Regardless of whatever grand promises your son made to you, Madame Jin, it would be best if he and my Shijie walked completely separate paths from this day forward!"

He was practically vibrating with rage, giving zero quarter in his delivery. Fortunately, Madame Jin was entirely consumed with soothing Jiang Yanli and paid his sharp tone no mind. Jin Zixun, however, wasn't about to let the slight slide, barking, "Wei Wuxian! My aunt is your elder! Where do you get off speaking to her with such unbridled arrogance?!"

Murmurs of agreement rippled through the onlookers. Wei Wuxian fired back, "My words weren't aimed at Madame Jin. Your cousin has repeatedly hurled vile insults at my Shijie; if the Yunmeng Jiang Sect swallowed that disrespect lying down, we’d have no right to call ourselves a prominent clan! Where is the arrogance in defending our own?!"

Jin Zixun let out a mocking sneer. "Where is the arrogance? Is there an inch of you that isn't arrogant?! On an auspicious day like the Grand Hunt of the Hundred Clans, you've certainly stolen the spotlight, haven't you? Swallowing a third of the mountain's quarry all by yourself—feeling pretty damn proud of yourself, aren't you?!"

Lan Wangji’s head tilted slightly, his tone quiet: "A third of the quarry?"

Seeing Lan Wangji speak up—a man widely rumored to despise Wei Wuxian's very existence—several frustrated cultivators in the crowd couldn't hold back any longer:

"Hanguang-jun, you have no idea! We spent half the morning scouring Phoenix Mountain, only to find that every single fierce corpse and vengeful wraith had vanished into thin air!"

"We sent a runner to ask Lianfang-zun at the observation stands, and he told us that barely half an incense stick after the hunt kicked off, a flute echoed through the ridges—and almost every corpse and ghost on this mountain walked straight into the Yunmeng Jiang camp of their own free will!"

"Out of the three major classes of quarry, only the beasts and monsters are left..."

"As for the undead? Wei Wuxian hijacked every last one of them for himself!"

Jin Zixun drove the point home: "Stealing everyone's game to pad your own glory—are you going to claim that isn't arrogant?!"

Understanding finally dawned on Wei Wuxian. It was just a bunch of sore losers throwing a tantrum. He chuckled, "Weren't you the one boasting at the gate? 'What does an opening shot prove? Let's see you put your money where your mouth is on the mountain!'"

Jin Zixun scoffed, "Relying on crooked, heretical tricks isn't true martial skill! Blowing a couple of notes on a flute—you call that putting your money where your mouth is?!"

Wei Wuxian put on a face of pure, amused bewilderment. "I didn't break any rules, so why doesn't it count? If it's that easy, why don't you try blowing a couple of notes and see if any fierce corpse gives a damn about following you?"

Jin Zixun spat, "Disregarding basic protocol is no better than dirty underhanded sabotage!"

Lan Wangji’s brow pinched into a sharp, displeased scowl. Madame Jin finally took notice of the escalating spat, cutting in with flat exhaustion: "Zixun, that's enough."

Wei Wuxian couldn't even be bothered to waste his breath on him, tossing back with a smirk, "Fine then. Clearly, I don't know what 'true skill' looks like. Why don't you pull some out, beat my score, and enlighten me?"

If he had the power to beat him, Jin Zixun wouldn't be standing here choking on his own bitter bile. Thrown into a stammering corner, his humiliation curdled into pure vitriol: "No wonder you see nothing wrong with your conduct—flouting the rules is second nature to you! You didn't wear a sword to the flower banquet, and you didn't wear one to the grand hunt today! On an occasion of this magnitude, you display zero manners and zero etiquette! Where do you think you're putting the rest of us who bothered dressing for the occasion?!"

Wei Wuxian didn't even grant him a glance. Turning his back entirely, he looked toward Lan Wangji with an easy grin. "Lan Zhan, almost forgot to mention—thanks for deflecting that sword strike earlier."

Seeing himself brushed aside like an insignificant insect, Jin Zixun ground his teeth so hard they nearly cracked, snarling:

"The upbringing of the Yunmeng Jiang Sect truly amounts to nothing more than this!"
